title: Same Letters, Any Order
statement:
Given two strings s and t, return true if t can be made by rearranging the letters of s, and false otherwise.

Every letter must be used exactly as many times as it appears: the counts must match, not just the set of letters.

examples.why: Both strings hold one each of b, e, l, o, w.
Both use only a and b, but s has two a's and t has one. Comparing sets of letters would wrongly say true.
Different lengths can never be rearrangements of each other.

constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Two strings are rearrangements of each other exactly when some "fingerprint" of them matches. Which fingerprint ignores order but keeps counts?
Sorting both strings gives one such fingerprint. Can you build one in a single pass instead?
Count each letter of s up and each letter of t down in one table of 26 counters. They match only if every counter ends at zero.

explain.intuition:
Order does not matter, counts do. So reduce each string to how many times each letter appears and compare those counts. With only 26 lowercase letters, an array of 26 integers is the whole fingerprint.

A neat way to compare: add 1 for each letter of s, subtract 1 for each letter of t. Any counter that is not zero at the end means one string has more of that letter.
steps: If the lengths differ, return false right away.
For each position i: add 1 to the counter for s[i] and subtract 1 from the counter for t[i].
Return true only if every counter is 0.
pitfalls: Comparing sets of letters: "aab" and "abb" have the same set but different counts.
Skipping the length check while counting only over s: extra letters at the end of t would never be looked at.

solutions.title: Sort both strings
solutions.idea: Rearrangements of each other become identical once sorted.

solutions.title: 26 counters, up and down
solutions.idea: Count letters of s up and letters of t down in one table; all zeros means the counts match.

followups: The strings may contain any Unicode characters. What replaces the array of 26?
Given many strings, group the ones that are rearrangements of each other. What key would you use?
